articleTitle: Cost effective management security and control
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Designing Secure Systems
abstract: The author outlines how security projects can go wrong. She details an approach which is both practical and proven to work in effectively designing security solutions to any IT systems. The approach is made up of five component stages: establish baseline security factors; identify constraints; identify and analyse the business and IT risks; recommend countermeasures to reduce identified risk factors (appropriate at either global or local level); and regularly update as business and IT changes.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Automatic user authentication and access control
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Designing Secure Systems
abstract: The designer of secure computer systems needs to ensure that only authorised users use the system. The alternative automatic or computer aided techniques must therefore be considered. This is especially the case in distributed computing systems. The author considers: passwords, PINs and biometrics. From the latter he considers: signature; fingerprint; voice pattern; retinal patterns; hand shape and typing rhythm.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Designing Secure Systems
abstract: Summary form only, as follows. Today the power of computing is in the hands of the users through linked microprocessors. There is therefore a need to evolve the security procedures appropriate to mainframes into the networked microprocessor arena. To effect good security practices requires, at least: training of people, particularly users and system designers; simple to use procedures and software; procedures which are effective to detect errors; and a commitment by all involved never to accept second best. The challenge to everyone involved in the development or use of systems in the future is to create secure user friendly systems where the security elements are willingly used.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Protecting your organisation's most valuable asset (LAN security)
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Designing Secure Systems
abstract: The dramatic adoption of PCs and local area networks (LANs) in the last seven years was driven by the need to share and distribute information. Now, organisations are starting to count the cost. There is a growing threat to your organisation from a lack of proper information security: a threat which will cause near crippling losses to about one in ten organisations. A major survey concluded that little was being done to protect information. It's time to face up to the lack of LAN security. The article introduces some new ideas which can lead to affordable, easily managed, secure open system solutions.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The design of a secure distributed system
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Designing Secure Systems
abstract: CHOTS stands for Corporate Headquarters Office Technology System and from the point of view of many of the users it is primarily an office automation system. CHOTS was, however, conceived as a secure infrastructure that supports communication betweeen users and both local and corporate applications and databases. The objective has been to give the user the same facilities that she would have in a large commercial organisation while at the same time protecting the data from unauthorised access by MOD staff as well as intruders. The author introduces the elements of secure distributed systems and how these are combined in a practical realisation based on the CHOTS experience.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Designing Secure Systems
abstract: The author outlines areas at risk from computer crime. The computer itself should aid the auditor. UK legislation may help in the future.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Designing Secure Systems
abstract: With the spread of the adoption of standards in commercial systems, where the operation of the computing environment may be essential to the success of a companies business, the need for inclusion of security in open system environments is becoming recognised. Across the areas of open system standardisation extensions to the base standards are being defined to facilitate secure interworking. These include: security extensions the EDIFACT EDI message standards; security for the IEE 1003 POSIX, UNIX based operating system interface standards; security facilities for OSI application standards such as the CCITT X.400 message handling system and X.500 directory system; the OSI network and transport layer communications security protocols as well as the IEEE 802 secure LAN standard; and the OSI physical layer encryption device interface. The paper outlines the approach taken in each of these areas and suggests the relative role of the different placements and forms of security.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Secure software: management control is a key issue
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Designing Secure Systems
abstract: The article provides a guide to the major issues involved in the production of secure software, and outlines an approach for ensuring that where it is of benefit, then security can be achieved without risk to overall IT programmes, with expenditure firmly under the control of project management. The approach is sufficiently general to be applicable to bespoke development, product-based approaches, and the addition of security to existing environments.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
